question:
Suppose a square piece of paper is folded in half vertically. The folded paper is then cut in half along the dashed line. Three rectangles are formed—a large one and two small ones. What is the ratio of the perimeter of one of the small rectangles to the perimeter of the large rectangle?

[Figure 1](figures/1989_AMC_8_Q24_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
Choose a length unit in which the original square has side \(4\). This is allowed because changing the unit multiplies both perimeters by the same amount and leaves their ratio unchanged.

Folding vertically in half makes a rectangle of height \(4\) and width \(2\). The cut shown runs vertically halfway across this folded rectangle, leaving two strips of width \(1\). The strip next to the fold unfolds into one rectangle of width \(2\). The other strip consists of two separate paper layers, giving two rectangles of width \(1\). All three pieces have height \(4\).

Each small rectangle therefore has perimeter \(2(4+1)=10\), while the large rectangle has perimeter \(2(4+2)=12\). The requested ratio is
\[
\frac{10}{12}=\boxed{\frac56},
\]
choice \(\mathrm{E}\).

edges.reason: Describing rectangle and square properties presupposes recognizing which plane shapes those names designate.

Written columns support perimeter arithmetic with larger dimensions. Adding decomposed lengths mentally gives the same result even for two-digit sides, so Gemini's chosen calculation does not establish column-method necessity.
The perimeter formulas use rectangle opposite-side equality and square side equality to combine their boundary lengths.

Division introduces equal sharing, a useful conceptual bridge. Folding one whole into equal paper parts establishes a unit fraction without division notation or the inverse-multiplication interpretation.

The criteria expressly find common factors and reduce until numerator and denominator are coprime. These are the common-factor contents of the endpoint; finding the greatest factor in a single step is only a shortcut and is outside this required scope.
edges.scope: Finding a shared divisor and recognizing the absence of a shared divisor above one when reducing to simplest form

edges.reason: Reduction replaces numerator and denominator by division by the same common factor, using the value-preserving fraction property.
edges.scope: dividing numerator and denominator by a common number

edges.reason: Fraction division prepares ratio values with fractional terms. The target expressly permits a simple ratio, and a whole-number pair such as 6 to 3 needs only ordinary division; no fraction-by-fraction division is universal.
